sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

- When working on pi topics, read the docs and examples, and follow .md cross-references before implementing
- Always read pi .md files completely and follow links to related docs (e.g., tui.md for TUI API details)
</docs>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

content.text:
You improve the program in /repo, a git repository, so that it scores better on a hidden evaluation. The task and how it is scored:

<spec>
## SPEC.md

# datenorm: normalize messy date mentions to ISO dates

Build a command-line program that reads free-text date mentions and returns the calendar date each one refers to, as `YYYY-MM-DD`, or `null` when the text does not name exactly one valid calendar date.

## Program contract

- Language: Python 3.14, **standard library only**. There is no network access: you cannot `pip install` anything.
- Entry point: `python3 -m datenorm`, run from the repository root.
- Input: JSON Lines on stdin. Each line is one item: `{"id": "<string>", "text": "<string>", "locale": "US" | "EU"}`.
- Output: for every input line, write exactly one JSON line to stdout, in input order: `{"id": "<same id>", "date": "YYYY-MM-DD"}` or `{"id": "<same id>", "date": null}`.
- The caller sends one line, then waits for its answer before sending the next. Flush stdout after every line and do not wait for end of input before answering.
- Never crash on bad input: unparseable text gets `"date": null`. Write nothing else to stdout (use stderr for logs).
- Latency: each answer should take well under 50 ms. Do not do heavy work per line.

The starter repository already contains a stub that answers `null` for everything.

## Interpretation rules

The reference date ("today") is **2024-06-15** (a Saturday). It only matters for relative expressions.

### ISO-like dates

Year first, always year-month-day: `2023-07-04`, `2023/07/04`, `2023.07.04`, `20230704`, `2023-07-04T13:45:00Z`, `2023-07-04 08:30`. A time part is ignored.

### Numeric dates with the year last

The `locale` field decides the order:

- `US`: month first. `07/04/2023` → 2023-07-04.
- `EU`: day first. `04/07/2023` → 2023-07-04.

Separators can be `/`, `-` or `.`, with or without leading zeros. A two-digit year `YY` maps to `20YY` when `YY` ≤ 68, else to `19YY` (`7/4/23` → 2023, `7/4/75` → 1975). If the locale's reading is not a valid date (for example month 13), the answer is `null`. Do not fall back to the other order.

### Month names

Month names and their common abbreviations can appear in **English, French, German or Spanish**, in any letter case, with or without a trailing period (`Sept.`, `févr.`). Accents can be missing (`fevrier`, `Marz`). Weekday names can appear and are ignored. English ordinal suffixes (`1st`, `2nd`, `3rd`, `4th`) and the French `1er` mark the day.

Examples of accepted shapes: `July 4, 2023`, `4 July 2023`, `Jul 4th 2023`, `Tuesday, July 4, 2023`, `4th of July, 2023`, `JUL-04-2023`, `2023 Jul 04`, `4 juillet 2023`, `1er mars 2022`, `4. Juli 2023`, `4 de julio de 2023`.

### Days written as words

English day numbers can be written as ordinal words, with or without a hyphen: `the twenty-first of March 2021`, `May first, 2020`, `March thirty first 2021`. The year is always written in digits.

### Relative expressions (English only)

Relative to today, 2024-06-15:

- `today`, `yesterday`, `tomorrow`, `the day before yesterday`, `the day after tomorrow`
- `N days|weeks ago`, `in N days|weeks`, `N days|weeks from now|from today`. `N` can be digits or an English number word from one to twenty (`three weeks ago`), and `a` means 1 (`a week ago`).
- `N months ago`, `in N months`: same day number in the target month, clamped to the last day of that month.
- `next <weekday>`: the first such weekday strictly after today. `last <weekday>`: the most recent such weekday strictly before today. `this <weekday>`: that weekday in the current Monday-to-Sunday week.

### Dates inside longer text

The text can be a sentence that contains one date among other numbers: invoice numbers, amounts, times, phone numbers, version strings. Extract the date. Numbers that are not part of a date must not be read as one.

### When the answer is null

- No date in the text.
- The date does not exist (`2023-02-30`, `February 29, 2023`, `31/04/2022` with `EU`).
- Something date-like that is not a calendar date: versions (`1.2.3`), phone numbers, times only, a month and year with no day (`March 2023`).

## Examples

These are illustrative and are not taken from the hidden evaluation data.

| text | locale | date |
|---|---|---|
| `2019-11-30` | US | `2019-11-30` |
| `11/30/19` | US | `2019-11-30` |
| `30.11.2019` | EU | `2019-11-30` |
| `Nov. 30th, 2019` | EU | `2019-11-30` |
| `30 novembre 2019` | EU | `2019-11-30` |
| `30. November 2019` | EU | `2019-11-30` |
| `the thirtieth of November 2019` | US | `2019-11-30` |
| `next Wednesday` | US | `2024-06-19` |
| `two weeks ago` | EU | `2024-06-01` |
| `Order 5521 shipped on 11/30/2019, total $84.10` | US | `2019-11-30` |
| `release 2.4.1 is out` | US | `null` |
| `November 31, 2019` | US | `null` |

## How you are evaluated

See `METRICS.md`. You never see the evaluation data: write code that generalizes from these rules, not code that memorizes examples.


## METRICS.md

# Metrics

A hidden runner starts `python3 -m datenorm` once in a fresh copy of your repository. It sends the evaluation items one line at a time and times each answer. A hidden scorer then compares the answers with gold dates.

## Primary metric

- `accuracy`: the share of items whose `date` equals the gold answer exactly. A gold `null` is matched only by `null`. A missing, late or malformed answer counts as wrong.

## Reported metrics

- `acc_<family>`: accuracy per input family. The families are `iso`, `numeric`, `textual_en`, `textual_intl`, `ordinal_words`, `relative`, `embedded` and `invalid` (gold is always `null` for `invalid`).
- `null_precision`: of the items you answered `null`, the share whose gold is `null`.
- `latency_query_p50_ms`, `latency_query_p95_ms`: per-answer latency in milliseconds, from sending a query to receiving its answer. The first answer is a warm-up and is not counted.
- `latency_total_s`: the summed answer time over all queries, in seconds.

## Hard gates

A version that fails a gate is never kept, whatever its accuracy.

- `schema_violations` must be 0. It counts answer lines that are not valid JSON, have the wrong `id`, have a `date` that is neither `null` nor a `YYYY-MM-DD` string, or are missing. A per-answer timeout of 5 seconds or a crash counts as missing.
- `latency_query_p95_ms` must stay under a cap.
</spec>

A copy of the spec is at /spec/spec. /spec/train is the only labeled data you get.

<targets>
Raise all of these in this attempt, one task per metric:
- accuracy: dev not measured, threshold 1.01, weight 1
</targets>

Workflow:
1. Research, at most a fifth of the time: run the program first, and score the starting code on train.
2. Plan: write /tmp/tasks.json, a JSON list of {task, check, status}, status `todo`, `done`, or `dropped` plus a `note`.
3. Implement.
4. Review: check each task, measure again, close the tasks.

How to work:
- Test on cases you write; you never get the evaluation data.
- Where the spec leaves an interpretation open, choose one on purpose and say which.
- How the keep works: each threshold metric earns min(value / threshold, 1) times its weight; the weighted score is their sum over the sum of weights. Thresholds and weights: accuracy ≥ 1.01 (weight 1). The change is kept only if its weighted score beats the current one by more than the noise margin of repeated runs.
- cost_per_item_usd and latency_total_s are measured for the report, not for the keep.
- Each run of the program gets 3 minutes in the evaluation; a longer one scores nothing. Evaluation inputs can be much longer than train's: leave room in token limits and timeouts.
- Packages: `uv add` in /repo, commit pyproject.toml and uv.lock, run with .venv/bin/python.
- Simpler is better.
- Write /tmp/notes.md for the next coder: at most 20 plain lines of checked facts (tools, limits, runtimes, train measurements, what failed and why); no claim about dev or test.
- Write /tmp/train-score.json: `before` and `after` objects of metric scores and the `command`; `why` if a metric fell. Score on train items no few-shot example comes from.
- Send long output to a file. Commit only as a checkpoint: the harness commits /repo as it stands.
- You have 10 minutes; the round ends at 2026-11-18T11:27:17.697Z. Check the clock (`date -u`) before you stop.
- End your final message with `APPROACH: <one sentence>`.
